title: Isolation movements benefits: attacking muscles more precisely
summary: NH argues compound lifts blur which muscles get worked (leverages, form differences, focus on strength), so isolation movements are essential for bodybuilding, especially for stubborn muscles. His lats did not grow from a 500 lb deadlift but did from slow pullovers and pull-ups. Do compounds for strength plus isolation for lagging parts.

claims.claim: Isolation movements are essential for bodybuilding and building a good physique.
Compound lifts make it hard to know which muscle is worked because leverages and proportions change activation: some people feel mostly chest on bench, others only triceps or front delts.
Activation ratios on compounds are broadly similar between individuals, but differences can still be significant enough to affect gains.
Small form differences, between people or within one person, change muscle activation in compound lifts.
Because compounds are done heavy and intense, you focus on strength rather than feeling the target muscle work.
He never feels his quads or gets a quad pump when squatting, yet built 26-inch legs from basically only squats; quads are his best body part.
A loaded working muscle grows even without mind-muscle connection, but for stubborn, ungifted muscles you may need to build that connection to activate them better.
Many compound-only lifters blame bad genetics for muscles that don't grow when the real cause is lack of direct work.
He ran a powerlifting program of only compounds and variations for 1.5 years; some body parts grew a lot while others didn't move.
When he hit his first 500 lb deadlift he had essentially no lats, contradicting the idea that deadlifts build lats; he wrongly blamed lat genetics.
Pullovers and pull-ups done with very slow tempo and low weight grew his lats far more than heavy deadlifts and rows.
Minimalists need to hear that isolation isn't only for arms and shoulders; other muscles important for strength aren't developed enough by compounds.
Do both: compounds for strength, compound variations (still great for hypertrophy), and isolation for the body parts that need it.
Use your genetic gifts to save time: if a muscle grows from compounds alone (his quads from squats), skip extra work for it and invest that time in isolating weak parts.
His body parts that need isolation: triceps, lats, traps, rear delts and parts of his forearms.

Telling someone they'll get a good back from a 700 lb deadlift is unrealistic; you can get good forearms with lighter weights via direct isolation, and many elite deadlifters still have small forearms.
Every program he writes, even for novices, includes isolation movements, because the earlier you start the better your physique looks long term.
